(kik. eR 8 eee The Reverend Joseph Silver Sr. who held the distinction of being the early organizer of the Holiness Church in the Eastern USA, guided the young couple into purchasing their first parcel of farmland and dwelling of sufficient size to accommodate their rapidly increasing family. Approximately 40 acres were purchased in the initial transaction, and was followed by the purchase of approximately 150 additional acres later. By the year 1920, this couple had achieved a status that became the envy of their neighbors and friends. Home ownership, land ownership, and a healthy family of eight children as of that date, constituted a prosperous farming business. One of the rewarding aspects of this couple’s blessing of prosperity could be seen in their simple but unique philosophy. They believed that sacrifice and hard work were cornerstones to success when these elements undergird a well defined purpose and determination to achieve. This philosophy could also be seen in the emphasis our parents placed on education, thrift, work ethics, religion, respect for oneself, and the respect for others. They considered the family as a unique social unit that is endowed with the responsibility of sustaining itself, and structured in such a way as to provide the leadership, discipline, and citizenship directions throughout one’s entire social life. As the years rolled by, the family and the farming enterprise increased and prospered. Another member was added to the family practically every year. As the family continued to increase, our parents sought to fulfil their obligation of passing onto the their children certain intrinsic values they felt would certainly be needed in order to compete successfully in an increasingly complex society. They felt that education for survival begins in the home. With this concept, a rather unique "Family-shared Work Assignment Program" was instituted. Our parents felt that each member of the family should, within the limits of his or her talent and capability, contribute to the general welfare of the whole family. Therefore, each family member was assigned a specific area of family living, and was held accountable for accomplishment of the family’s performance goals. Two boys were held responsible for feeding and caring for the teams of mules; two were caretakers of the hogs; one was to care for the chickens; one was held responsible for milking the cows and processing the milk and butter; two boys were assigned to the vegetable garden; one of the girls did the laundry; one girl served as assistant cook and the others were assigned minor jobs in the cooperative-living plan. Everybody, however, was required to make-up their own beds in the morning, go to Sunday school and church on Sundays, be home before sundown, and if one were of the acceptable courting age, he had to be at home before 10:00 p.m. The boys were allowed to try their hand at enterprising. One sold the Grit Newspaper; one sold Cloverine Healing Salves; one sold garden seeds; one handled dairy products; one ran a small country store; one raised squabs and poultry, and another did some roadside bartering of roasted peanuts and peanut candy along the roadside with laborers who would travel to and from their jobs at the small country town of Delmar, North Carolina, located by the railroad adjacent to our farm. No one got rich in these small ventures, but much was learned and ambitions stimulated as a result of the tolerance and character-development skills of these parents. 4 ~ Me e b rrr 20 «rr rr i ee ME ee ae ee ee rrr re FF ™ — a mies: amc eo ee
